messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rodrigo is a 53-year-old divorced tax consultant of Colombian descent who was referred for psychological assessment following a disclosure made to his primary care physician. His PCL-5 score of 57 places him firmly in the severe range for PTSD, and the picture that has emerged across the intake and first two sessions is one of a man whose inner world has been quietly collapsing for some time.

The precipitating event occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Rodrigo had been working late and stopped at a convenience store on his way home. In the parking lot, he witnessed two officers detaining a young man — a scene that escalated with startling speed into something he cannot fully reconstruct in sequence. What he does remember with terrible clarity is the young man's face pressed against the asphalt, a gash across his temple bleeding freely, and the sound the man made — a low, involuntary sound that Rodrigo describes as not quite human. He was not physically harmed himself, but he was ordered to the ground as well, held there for nearly twenty minutes while officers established what had happened. He was eventually released without explanation or apology. He drove home in silence and did not speak of it to anyone for three months.

In the weeks that followed, Rodrigo noticed that his body had developed its own vocabulary for the event before his mind had caught up. A bruise on a colleague's forearm, glimpsed during a meeting, sent a wave of nausea through him so severe he had to excuse himself. The sight of any visible injury — a cut, a scrape, a bandage on a stranger's hand — became almost unbearable, pulling him immediately back to the parking lot, to the blood, to the young man's face. These intrusive moments do not arrive as coherent memories so much as fragments with physical force: a sudden tightening in his own jaw, a dull ache that spreads across the side of his face where, he notes almost incidentally, he had pressed against the pavement. This somatic echo — pain without injury — is among the more disorienting aspects of his presentation. When these triggers fire, they do not merely distress him; they confirm something he has come to believe with quiet, terrible certainty: that there is something about him, some quality he cannot name, that drew the officers' attention that night, that placed him on the ground, that made it happen. The intrusive images do not feel like bad luck revisiting him — they feel like evidence.

That appraisal — that he is somehow culpable, marked, fundamentally different from people who move through the world without incident — has reorganized how Rodrigo inhabits space. He had come to believe that ordinary environments were legible only to people who had not been exposed as he had been. Unfamiliar places, in particular, feel like traps he cannot read. He no longer accepts client meetings at locations he has not visited before; twice in the past year he has declined work that required travel, offering billing conflicts as the reason. His practice, once growing steadily, has contracted. In every room he enters — his office building, the parking garage, the grocery store — he locates the exits before he allows himself to sit or stand still, and he checks behind him with a regularity that has become automatic, a habit so ingrained he sometimes does it mid-sentence with a client. This hypervigilant scanning, far from reassuring him, keeps the threat alive. The very act of searching for danger confirms that danger is present, and that confirmation loops back into the belief that he is someone for whom the world is not safe — not because the world is dangerous, but because something about him invites it. The surveillance and the self-blame feed each other, and in feeding each other they keep the triggers close: a flash of someone's bruised arm, a twinge of pain in his cheek, a face that reminds him of the young man on the ground, and the whole architecture shudders.

Rodrigo lives alone since his divorce, which preceded the incident by several years, and he has allowed most of his friendships to thin to nothing. He describes feeling sealed off from people in a way he cannot explain to them, and no longer tries to. What finally brought him to his physician was a single sentence he wrote in a personal journal and then could not stop rereading: that he was no longer certain his life was worth living. He does not present as acutely suicidal, but the sentence frightened him enough to act. What he says he wants most is to stop feeling like the cause of his own suffering.
